title: Crossmatching & Antibody Screening

references.label: AABB Technical Manual
references.publisher: Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies (AABB)

references.label: CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

summary: Antibody screening tests a patient's plasma against a panel of reagent red cells carrying known, clinically significant antigens to detect unexpected (non-ABO) antibodies before transfusion; crossmatching then directly tests the patient's plasma against the specific donor unit(s) intended for transfusion.
explanation: Antibody screening uses reagent screening cells selected to express the antigens most commonly associated with clinically significant hemolytic transfusion reactions or hemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn; a positive screen triggers antibody identification (testing against an extended panel to determine which specific antibody is present) before a safe unit can be selected. Crossmatching serves as a final direct check between patient plasma and the actual donor unit: an immediate-spin (or electronic, in eligible low-risk settings) crossmatch mainly confirms ABO compatibility, while a full antiglobulin (indirect Coombs) crossmatch also detects clinically significant antibodies reacting against that specific donor's cells, extending the sensitivity beyond ABO alone. Together, ABO/Rh typing (forward and reverse), antibody screening, and crossmatching form layered, complementary safety checks — no single step is considered sufficient alone before red cell transfusion.

commonMisconceptions: Assuming ABO/Rh typing alone is sufficient to safely release blood — a negative antibody screen and compatible crossmatch are additional required safety layers precisely because clinically significant antibodies beyond ABO/Rh do occur.
